name: Qatar
summary: Qatar Central Bank (QCB) licenses and supervises onshore banks, including AML/CFT, customer protection and technology risk, through its Instructions to Banks, regulations and circulars. The Qatar Financial Information Unit receives suspicious transaction reports, the National Counter Terrorism Committee circulates terrorist designations, the National Cyber Security Agency administers the personal data law, and the General Tax Authority is CRS competent authority. The Qatar Financial Centre has its own regulator (QFCRA) and is not covered here. The QCB AML/CFT Instructions (annual AML/CFT training), the Technology Risks Regulation (security awareness at induction and yearly) and the Data Handling and Protection Regulation were opened and confirmed.

regulators.role: Separate regulator for firms authorised in the Qatar Financial Centre, with its own rules; not covered by the mappings in this file.

programs.title: Qatar | AML/CFT Compliance under Law No. 20 of 2019 and the QCB AML/CFT Instructions
programs.why: The QCB AML/CFT Instructions issued under Law 20 of 2019 make an ongoing AML/CFT training programme a core part of every bank's AML/CFT programme. All officers and employees must be trained at least once a year and whenever needed, on their legal duties, ML/TF risks and how to report suspicions, with training needs reviewed regularly and records kept for 10 years.

references.title: Law No. (20) of 2019 on Combating Money Laundering and Terrorism Financing
references.provision: Articles 6-7 (risk assessment and risk-based internal policies, procedures and controls)
references.note: English text of the AML/CFT law, which repealed Law No. 4 of 2010. Chapter 3 sets the preventive duties of financial institutions: risk assessment, risk-based internal controls, due diligence, PEPs, correspondent banking, record keeping and prompt reporting to the FIU. Amended by Decree-Law No. 19 of 2021 (amendment published on the QFIU site in Arabic only).

references.title: Anti-Money Laundering and Combating Terrorism Financing Instructions for Financial Institutions (May 2020 Edition)
references.note: Section 21.2 requires an ongoing AML/CFT training programme for officers and employees, at least annually for all staff and whenever needed, covering legal duties, ML/TF threats and red flags and internal STR procedures, tailored to roles and risk; 21.3 requires regular reviews of training needs considered by the board; 22.1 keeps training records for 10 years.

The QCB AML/CFT Instructions oblige every employee to report suspicions to the MLRO and require the annual AML/CFT training to teach staff how to make effective internal STRs, so STR training is mandatory. The QFIU's April 2024 instructions explain how reports are made.

They require directors to be competent and trained, but set no general governance course for all staff, so the entry stays at competence.

programs.why: The 2015 QCB governance principles require the board to assess nominees' eligibility and ability to serve, and the QCB AML/CFT Instructions require screening of senior officials, MLROs and controlled functions for character, knowledge and skills. These are competence and fitness requirements, not training duties; the 2022 governance instructions could not be opened.

references.title: Legislation (QCB legislation index, including Circular No. 25/2022 Governance Instructions in Banks and Circular No. 2/2023)
references.note: QCB index of laws, instructions and circulars; lists the 2022 governance instructions for banks and their 2023 amendment. Not opened: qcb.gov.qa certificate chain cannot be verified.

references.title: Circular No. 68/2015: Corporate Governance Principles for Banks
references.note: 2015 governance principles: the board must give each new director a formal, tailored induction and keep all directors trained on the bank's business and governance, with the nomination committee overseeing director training. QCB Circular 25/2022 (governance instructions in banks, amended by Circular 2/2023) is reported to have replaced this text; the 2022 instructions could not be opened.

references.title: Anti-Money Laundering and Combating Terrorism Financing Instructions for Financial Institutions (May 2020 Edition)
references.note: Higher-impact individuals (senior officials, MLRO and deputy, controlled functions) must be screened for character, knowledge, skills and integrity before appointment and on a continuing basis.

programs.title: Qatar | QCB Customer Protection Instructions
programs.why: The QCB Instructions to Banks make QCB customer protection instructions binding and allow QCB action for breaches, and the QCB Customer Protection Department handles complaints and issues directives. No training duty was found in the opened texts, so the entry is competence.

references.title: Instructions to Banks, Part VIII, Second: Banking Consumer Services Protection Department
references.note: 2013 edition of the Instructions to Banks: QCB set up a department to protect bank customers and receive complaints, each bank's liaison officer handles customer complaints, answers them within about a week and keeps complaint files, and QCB customer protection instructions are binding with QCB action for breaches.

references.title: Customer Protection Department
references.note: QCB page describing its Customer Protection Department, which receives and handles customer complaints against financial institutions impartially, issues customer protection policies and directives, and lists complaint channels (email, hotline, in person).

programs.title: Qatar | Transparent Disclosure of Fees and Product Risks
programs.why: The QCB Instructions to Banks require banks doing investment business for customers to explain the risks in writing, specify the commissions charged and send regular statements. Staff selling these products need to know the rules, but no training duty was found.

references.title: Instructions to Banks, Part VII, Chapter Four: Relation with Customers
references.note: 2013 edition: banks doing investment business for customers must explain the related risks in writing, set out the commissions they charge, send at least monthly statements and obtain customer approval before operations that conflict with the customer's interests.

programs.title: Qatar | Customer Complaint Handling
programs.why: The QCB Instructions to Banks assign customer complaints to a bank liaison officer who must answer within about a week and keep complaint files, and the QCB Customer Protection Department receives escalated complaints. No training duty was found.

references.title: Instructions to Banks, Part VIII, Second: Banking Consumer Services Protection Department
references.note: 2013 edition of the Instructions to Banks: QCB set up a department to protect bank customers and receive complaints, each bank's liaison officer handles customer complaints, answers them within about a week and keeps complaint files, and QCB customer protection instructions are binding with QCB action for breaches.

references.title: Customer Protection Department
references.note: QCB page describing its Customer Protection Department, which receives and handles customer complaints against financial institutions impartially, issues customer protection policies and directives, and lists complaint channels (email, hotline, in person).

programs.title: Qatar | Escalation of Complaints to the QCB Customer Protection Department
programs.why: The QCB Customer Protection Department receives customer complaints against financial institutions and handles them impartially; staff should know the route and respond to QCB requests. No training duty was found.

references.title: Customer Protection Department
references.note: QCB page describing its Customer Protection Department, which receives and handles customer complaints against financial institutions impartially, issues customer protection policies and directives, and lists complaint channels (email, hotline, in person).

references.title: Instructions to Banks, Part VIII, Second: Banking Consumer Services Protection Department
references.note: 2013 edition of the Instructions to Banks: QCB set up a department to protect bank customers and receive complaints, each bank's liaison officer handles customer complaints, answers them within about a week and keeps complaint files, and QCB customer protection instructions are binding with QCB action for breaches.

programs.title: Qatar | Customer Data Confidentiality under the QCB Data Handling and Protection Regulation
programs.why: The QCB Data Handling and Protection Regulation requires financial institutions to give employees and relevant stakeholders the training and awareness needed to keep their knowledge of data privacy, classification and handling up to date, and requires training on data security, data protection and privacy as part of data processing controls.

references.title: Data Handling and Protection Regulation
references.note: Training and awareness so staff regularly update their knowledge of data privacy, classification, handling, stewardship and backup; systems and controls must include training on data security, protection and privacy. Also requires a Data Privacy Officer.

references.title: Law No. 13 of 2016 - Personal Data Privacy Protection
references.note: Personal Data Privacy Protection Law, administered by the NCSA. Controllers must process data lawfully and apply proportionate security precautions; processors must notify controllers of breaches. Not opened: the NCSA page loads its content by script and returns only an empty shell to plain HTTP requests.

programs.title: Qatar | Information Security Awareness under the QCB Technology Risks Regulation
programs.why: The QCB Technology Risks Regulation requires banks to run a security awareness programme: information security training for new employees at induction, refreshers at least annually for all staff, content reviewed every year, effectiveness assessments after training and records of attendance and acknowledgement.

references.title: Technology Risks Regulation for Banks (January 2018)
references.note: Banks must run a funded security awareness programme; new staff get it at induction and everyone gets a refresher at least yearly, including how to recognise social engineering. Content is reviewed annually, effectiveness is assessed and attendance and acknowledgements are kept; senior management and directors get training on cyber threats.

programs.title: Qatar | Cybersecurity Awareness for Bank Staff
programs.why: The QCB Technology Risks Regulation requires cyber security awareness training for all employees and long-term contractors, at induction and at least annually, updated each year for current attack techniques and monitored for completion, with attendance and acknowledgement records.

references.title: Technology Risks Regulation for Banks (January 2018)
references.note: Banks must run a funded security awareness programme; new staff get it at induction and everyone gets a refresher at least yearly, including how to recognise social engineering. Content is reviewed annually, effectiveness is assessed and attendance and acknowledgements are kept; senior management and directors get training on cyber threats.

programs.title: Qatar | Cybersecurity Risk Management under QCB Technology Risk Rules
programs.why: The QCB Technology Risks Regulation requires board-approved cyber security policy, strategy and budget, board and senior management oversight of technology risk, and a separate information security function. These require competent staff but do not prescribe a separate risk management course.

references.title: Technology Risks Regulation for Banks (January 2018)
references.note: Board approval of cyber policy, strategy and budget; annual policy review; IT and technology-risk committees; a dedicated information security function and security programme.

programs.title: Qatar | Personal Data Privacy Protection Law (Law No. 13 of 2016)
programs.why: The QCB Data Handling and Protection Regulation requires financial institutions to process personal data in compliance with Law No. 13 of 2016 on Personal Data Privacy Protection. The law itself could not be opened (NCSA page is script-rendered; Al Meezan could not be read), so the entry stays at competence.

references.title: Law No. 13 of 2016 - Personal Data Privacy Protection
references.note: Personal Data Privacy Protection Law, administered by the NCSA. Controllers must process data lawfully and apply proportionate security precautions; processors must notify controllers of breaches. Not opened: the NCSA page loads its content by script and returns only an empty shell to plain HTTP requests.

references.title: Data Handling and Protection Regulation
references.note: Personal data must be processed in compliance with Law No. 13 of 2016 on Personal Data Privacy Protection, which is listed among the applicable references.

programs.title: Qatar | Phishing and Social Engineering Prevention
programs.why: The QCB Technology Risks Regulation requires the annual security awareness refresher to train employees to recognise social engineering attempts and not disclose information, and requires banks to educate users on email threats, phishing and social engineering and to report phishing incidents to the QCB.

references.title: Technology Risks Regulation for Banks (January 2018)
references.note: Annual refresher covering social engineering; users educated on suspicious emails and not giving out personal or financial data; anti-phishing controls and notification of phishing incidents to QCB.

programs.title: Qatar | Cyber Incident Identification and Reporting to the QCB
programs.why: The QCB Technology Risks Regulation integrates incident management into security awareness training: all users must be trained to report incidents to the incident team. Critical incidents must be reported to QCB and relevant authorities within one hour of identification, and the response plan tested every year.

references.title: Technology Risks Regulation for Banks (January 2018)
references.note: Internal and external incident communication plan; all users trained to report incidents; critical incidents reported to QCB and authorities within 1 hour; annual testing of the escalation and response plan.

programs.title: Qatar | Personal Data Breach Management
programs.why: The QCB Data Handling and Protection Regulation requires data breaches and privacy breaches to be treated as incidents, reported to QCB and to the NCSA and Ministry of Interior, assessed for impact and, where needed, notified to customers. Incident handlers need this knowledge, but no separate training is prescribed.

references.title: Law No. 13 of 2016 - Personal Data Privacy Protection
references.note: Personal Data Privacy Protection Law, administered by the NCSA. Controllers must process data lawfully and apply proportionate security precautions; processors must notify controllers of breaches. Not opened: the NCSA page loads its content by script and returns only an empty shell to plain HTTP requests.

references.title: Data Handling and Protection Regulation
references.note: Classify breaches as incidents, report them to QCB and other Qatari authorities including the NCSA and Ministry of Interior, assess impact, decide on customer notification and act to limit harm.

programs.title: Qatar | Cybersecurity Awareness for Senior Management and the Board
programs.why: The QCB Technology Risks Regulation requires that senior management and board members be made aware of cyber threats through appropriate training sessions, and gives the board responsibility for approving cyber policy, strategy and budget. No frequency is set for the board sessions.

references.title: Technology Risks Regulation for Banks (January 2018)
references.note: Senior management and directors must receive training sessions on cyber threats; the board approves the cyber security policy, strategy and budget and establishes the security function.

programs.title: Qatar | Credit Risk Management under the QCB Credit Risk Instructions
programs.why: QCB requires each bank to run credit risk under a board-approved strategy and policies, reviewed at least yearly, with sound credit-granting, administration, measurement and control processes. The instructions require that all relevant staff and officers clearly understand the credit strategy and policies and that credit staff and committee members have the skills and experience for the risks they handle. No separate course is prescribed, so this is a competence duty.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (Arabic edition): Part One, Chapter Two, First: Credit Risk Management
references.provision: Part One, Chapter Two, First, items 1 to 6
references.note: Board approves and reviews credit strategy and policies (reflecting risk appetite); management must make sure staff and officers understand them and follow defined credit-granting and monitoring procedures.

references.title: Instructions to Banks (September 2013, fifteenth edition): Part VII, Chapter One: Banking Risk
references.provision: Second (Credit and Financing Risk), E: Credit Risk Management, items 1/6 and 3/4
references.note: English text of the same instructions (Circular 32/2011): staff must clearly understand credit policy, and banks must ensure the capability and skills of credit staff and committee members.

programs.title: Qatar | Liquidity Risk Management, LCR and NSFR under QCB Instructions
programs.why: QCB applies the Basel III liquidity standards: banks must hold a liquidity coverage ratio and a net stable funding ratio of at least 100 percent, report maturity ladders and funding concentrations, and keep a board-approved liquidity policy with stress tests and a contingency funding plan. Staff who manage and report liquidity need working knowledge of these rules; no specific training is prescribed.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (Arabic edition): Part One, Chapter One, Second: Market and Liquidity Risk Management
references.provision: Part One, Chapter One, Second, items 1-5 and 11
references.note: LCR and NSFR minimums of 100 percent (LCR calculated daily), maturity ladder and funding concentration reporting, credit-to-deposit ratio, and general rules on a liquidity policy with stress testing and contingency plans.

references.title: Instructions to Banks (September 2013, fifteenth edition): Part VII, Chapter One: Banking Risk
references.note: Earlier English text (Circular 52/2008): board-approved liquidity policy, contingency plans reviewed at least yearly, liquidity stress testing and daily monitoring.

programs.title: Qatar | Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book under QCB IRRBB Instructions
programs.why: QCB implementing instructions on interest rate risk in the banking book require a board-set risk appetite, an IRRBB framework run through ALCO with periodic independent review, at least quarterly reporting to the board, and board members with enough expertise to understand and challenge IRRBB reports. This is a competence duty for the board and ALM functions.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (Arabic edition): Annex 16: Implementing instructions on managing interest rate risk for positions held other than for trading (banking book)
references.provision: Annex 16, role of the board of directors
references.note: Board must understand the nature and level of IRRBB, receive at least quarterly reports, and its members must have sufficient expertise to review them; banks need an IRRBB framework with independent reviews.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (index page, Arabic)
references.note: QCB index of the 2024 edition of the Instructions to Banks, published in Arabic only; lists every chapter and annex with its PDF.

programs.title: Qatar | Capital Adequacy under QCB Basel III Instructions and ICAAP
programs.why: QCB sets capital adequacy for national conventional banks on revised Basel III (Pillar 1), with capital buffers, extra requirements for domestic systemically important banks, a leverage ratio, an internal capital adequacy assessment process (Pillar 2) and Pillar 3 disclosure. Staff who compute, report and plan capital need competence in these rules; no training duty is stated.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (Arabic edition): Part One, Chapter One, First: Capital Adequacy Framework
references.provision: Part One, Chapter One, First, items 1 to 3
references.note: Revised Basel III Pillar 1 ratio, countercyclical buffer, D-SIB requirements, leverage ratio, Additional Tier 1 instruments, ICAAP guidance and IRRBB, and capital for foreign bank branches.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (index page, Arabic)
references.note: QCB index of the 2024 edition of the Instructions to Banks, published in Arabic only; lists every chapter and annex with its PDF.

references.title: Instructions to Banks (September 2013, fifteenth edition): Part XII, First: Capital Adequacy Ratio
references.note: Older English reporting text on the capital adequacy ratio return (2013 edition).

programs.title: Qatar | Stress Testing and Scenario Analysis in Qatari Banks
programs.why: Stress testing runs through several QCB instruments: liquidity stress tests feeding contingency funding plans, stress testing within the ICAAP, and the governance principles that require banks to run stress tests and scenario analysis as part of risk assessment. These build a competence need for risk and treasury teams; no stand-alone stress testing course is required.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (Arabic edition): Part One, Chapter One, Second: Market and Liquidity Risk Management
references.provision: Part One, Chapter One, Second, item 11 (general liquidity instructions)
references.note: Liquidity policy must cover normal and stressed conditions, with stress tests and contingency funding plans built on their results.

references.title: Circular No. 68/2015: Corporate Governance Principles for Banks
references.note: 2015 governance principles: banks must run stress tests and scenario analyses to identify exposures under adverse conditions.

references.title: Instructions to Banks (September 2013, fifteenth edition): Part XIII, Annex: Guidance on Basel Capital Adequacy Pillar II Application (SREP and ICAAP)
references.note: English text of the Pillar 2 guidance, including stress testing within the ICAAP (2013 edition; the 2024 edition carries it as Annex 15 in Arabic).

programs.title: Qatar | Large Exposures and Credit Concentration under QCB Instructions
programs.why: QCB's large exposures instructions define connected counterparties, set how exposures are measured, cap exposure to a single counterparty or connected group (generally 25 percent of Tier 1 capital) and require reporting of large exposures. Bankers and risk staff must identify connected groups correctly; this is a competence duty without prescribed training.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (Arabic edition): Part One, Chapter Two, Second: Large Credit Exposures
references.provision: Part One, Chapter Two, Second, items 1 to 5
references.note: Scope, definition of large exposures and connected counterparties, exposure measurement, limits for customers and banks, reporting and transition (Circulars 20/2018 and 17/2019).

programs.title: Qatar | Country and Transfer Risk under QCB Instructions
programs.why: National banks must keep exposures to foreign countries within QCB limits that depend on country risk category, apply core principles of country risk management, and classify and provide for country exposures. Staff who book or monitor cross-border exposures need to know these limits; no training is prescribed.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (Arabic edition): Part One, Chapter Two, Third: Country Risk and Transfer Risk
references.provision: Part One, Chapter Two, Third, items A to E
references.note: Definitions of country and transfer risk, maximum exposure limits abroad, principles for managing country risk, and classification and provisioning (Circulars 97/2015 and 104/2015).

programs.title: Qatar | Outsourcing and Cloud Risk Management
programs.why: The QCB Technology Risks Regulation requires a management-approved cloud policy, and the QCB Cloud Computing Regulation (in force 15 April 2024) sets governance, due diligence, contract, continuity and exit requirements for cloud arrangements. No separate training duty was found, so the entry is competence.

references.title: Technology Risks Regulation for Banks (January 2018)
references.note: Banks must have an approved, periodically reviewed cloud computing policy covering what applications and data are hosted in the cloud and the related controls.

references.title: Cloud Computing Regulation
references.note: QCB regulation on cloud use by QCB-licensed entities, in force from 15 April 2024: governance and strategy, due diligence on cloud providers, contract terms including sub-contracting notice, annual assessments, data location and consent under Law 13 of 2016, continuity and exit planning.

programs.title: Qatar | Business Continuity Management
programs.why: The QCB Technology Risks Regulation makes a senior BCM committee responsible for BCM training and awareness across the bank, and requires annual BCP testing including simulation tests that train personnel in post-incident and crisis roles, plus four unannounced drills a year. The duty targets staff with BCM roles.

references.title: Technology Risks Regulation for Banks (January 2018)
references.note: Head of BCM and a senior committee own BCM training and awareness; BIA and testing at least annually; table-top, simulation (to train crisis roles), technical and DR tests; at least four unplanned drills per year.

references.title: Cloud Computing Regulation
references.note: QCB regulation on cloud use by QCB-licensed entities, in force from 15 April 2024: governance and strategy, due diligence on cloud providers, contract terms including sub-contracting notice, annual assessments, data location and consent under Law 13 of 2016, continuity and exit planning.

programs.title: Qatar | Credit Classification and Provisioning under QCB Rules and IFRS 9
programs.why: QCB sets credit classification categories (including a stage 2 'accounts with remarks' category), minimum provisions, collateral valuation, rules for upgrading non-performing accounts, write-offs and data reporting, alongside expected credit loss provisioning under IFRS 9. Staff who grade loans or compute provisions need to apply these rules consistently; no specific training is required.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (Arabic edition): Part One, Chapter Two, Sixth: Classification of Credit Accounts and Provisioning
references.provision: Part One, Chapter Two, Sixth, items 1 to 5
references.note: Performing and non-performing categories, provision calculation, collateral valuation, provisioning under IFRS requirements checked by the external auditor, QCB notice before upgrading accounts, and write-offs.

references.title: Instructions to Banks (September 2013, fifteenth edition): Part VII, Chapter One: Banking Risk
references.provision: Second (Credit and Financing Risk), First: Credit Facility Classification and Provision Determination
references.note: Older English text of the classification and provisioning rules.

programs.title: Qatar | Qatar Credit Bureau Reporting
programs.why: QCB established the Qatar Credit Bureau in 2008 and requires each bank to nominate a compliance officer as its contact person and to submit accurate credit data in the bureau's formats, using validation tools to correct errors before submission. Staff who own bureau data need to know the reporting rules; this is a competence duty.

references.title: Instructions to Banks (September 2013, fifteenth edition): Part IX: Qatar Credit Bureau
references.note: Each bank names a compliance officer as contact with the bureau and submits validated credit data (Circulars 62/2009 and 48/2010). The 2024 Arabic edition was not checked for this part.

programs.title: Qatar | Salary-Backed Consumer Lending Limits under QCB Instructions
programs.why: QCB caps consumer credit granted against salary (maximum amounts, share of salary deducted, tenor and interest or profit rate rules), sets controls on rescheduling such loans and on early repayment fees, and requires fair and transparent advertising that shows the annual rate. Front-line and approval staff must apply these limits correctly; no training is prescribed.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (Arabic edition): Part One, Chapter Two, Fifth: Credit Granted against Salary
references.provision: Part One, Chapter Two, Fifth, items 1 to 7
references.note: Definitions, maximum limits and general controls, rescheduling, interest or return rules, early repayment commission and advertising of the annual rate (Circular 36/2011 and later amendments).

programs.title: Qatar | Real Estate Finance Controls under QCB Instructions
audience: Mortgage and real estate lending staff
programs.why: QCB sets an overall ceiling on each bank's net real estate finance risk relative to capital and reserves, controls on granting real estate finance, rules on enforcing collateral and periodic reporting with prescribed forms. Real estate lending and valuation staff must know these limits; this is a competence duty.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (Arabic edition): Part One, Chapter Two, Fourth: Real Estate Finance Controls and Risks
references.provision: Part One, Chapter Two, Fourth, items 1 to 6
references.note: Definitions, overall real estate finance risk ceiling, controls on granting, execution on collateral, general instructions and periodic returns (Circular 85/2010, amended by Circular 7/2023).

programs.title: Qatar | SME Definition, Financing and Reporting under QCB Instructions
audience: SME and business banking relationship managers
programs.why: QCB issued a standard definition of small and medium enterprises for the banking sector, requires periodic SME reporting, and urges banks to widen products and services for SMEs. Business banking and reporting staff need to classify SME customers correctly; no training duty is stated.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (Arabic edition): Part One, Chapter Two, Seventh: Other Credit Risk Instructions and Controls
references.provision: Part One, Chapter Two, Seventh, item 1 (SMEs)
references.note: Standard SME definition based on employees and turnover, SME reports, and bank support for SME financing; the same section also covers overdrafts, contract terms, foreign currency credit and collateral.

programs.title: Qatar | Account Opening Documentation under QCB Instructions
programs.why: QCB specifies the information, documents and contracts banks must collect when opening personal deposit accounts for residents and non-residents, the account opening procedure, a single main account per customer, the treatment of resident and non-resident accounts and the misuse of personal accounts for business. Account opening staff must follow these rules alongside AML due diligence; no training is prescribed.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (Arabic edition): Part One, Chapter Six, First: Customer Deposit Accounts
references.provision: Part One, Chapter Six, First, items 1, 2, 6 and 7
references.note: Required customer information, documents and contracts, account opening procedures, resident and non-resident accounts and use of personal accounts for business (Circular 103/2013 and later circulars, including 1/2025 and 2/2025).

programs.title: Qatar | Dormant Deposits and Unclaimed Balances under QCB Instructions
programs.why: QCB rules govern how banks identify and handle dormant deposit accounts, uncashed bank cheques and transfers, unpaid dividends, matured customer investments, unidentified amounts and unclaimed safe deposit contents. Operations staff must apply these steps to protect customers' money; this is a competence duty.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (Arabic edition): Part One, Chapter Six, Second: Dormant Deposits and Unclaimed Amounts
references.provision: Part One, Chapter Six, Second, items 1 and 2
references.note: General rules and treatment of dormant accounts, stale cheques and drafts, unpaid dividends, matured investments, unidentified amounts and unclaimed safe deposit box contents.

references.title: Instructions to Banks (September 2013, fifteenth edition): Part VII, Chapter Five: Dormant Deposits and Unclaimed Accounts
references.note: Older English text of the dormant accounts rules (2013 edition).

programs.title: Qatar | QCB Payment and Settlement Systems Rules for Banks
programs.why: QCB's instructions set the rules banks follow in the clearing house and the interbank payment and settlement systems, including cut-off times, the SWIFT message types and fields to use, and the bank's liability for wrong messages. Payments staff must apply these rules; no training is prescribed.

references.title: Instructions to Banks (September 2013, fifteenth edition): Part III, Chapter Two: Cheques, Clearing House and Payment Systems
references.note: Daily interbank payments through QCB, message formats and cut-off times, and bank responsibility for incorrect messages (2013 edition; the 2024 Arabic edition was not checked for this part).

programs.title: Qatar | Bank Branch and ATM Security under QCB Instructions
programs.why: QCB requires physical security measures in banks and at ATMs: strong rooms, alarms, surveillance cameras meeting set specifications, secure cash transport, key control, protection of records and a security committee of senior officials. QCB also advises senior management to brief managers and senior officials on handling customers calmly in abnormal situations. This is advice and a control framework rather than a training rule.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (Arabic edition): Part One, Chapter Eight, Ninth: Security and Safety in Banks and ATMs
references.provision: Part One, Chapter Eight, Ninth, items A to D (including guidance items 13 and 15)
references.note: Security guidance and specifications for banks and ATMs, a security committee of senior officials, and QCB's advice that managers be briefed on dealing with customers in abnormal circumstances (Circulars 195/2007 and 52/2011).

programs.title: Qatar | Payment Services and E-Money under the QCB Payment Services Regulation
programs.why: The 2021 Payment Services Regulation lets licensed banks keep offering payment services without a new licence but requires QCB approval for new ones and applies its operating rules (risk management, information security, outsourcing, agents, KYC, customer protection and e-money conditions) to banks. It requires skilled staff and other resources to run the service reliably; no training is prescribed.

references.title: Payment Services Regulation (Licensing and Regulating Payment Service Providers)
references.note: Licensed banks are exempt payment service providers but need approval for new services and must follow sections 10 to 24; licensees must have skilled manpower and meet e-money conditions.

programs.title: Qatar | Cheque Settlement and Clearing under Qatari Law and QCB Rules
programs.why: The Trade Law, as amended in 2010, makes a cheque payable on presentation and bars a bank from paying a post-dated cheque before its date, and sets presentation periods. QCB's instructions restate these rules and govern the clearing house. Tellers and clearing staff must apply them; this is a competence duty.

references.title: Instructions to Banks (September 2013, fifteenth edition): Part III, Chapter Two: Cheques, Clearing House and Payment Systems
references.provision: First: Cheques, item 1; Second: Clearing House
references.note: Cheque settlement under Trade Law articles 580 and 581 (as amended by Law No. 7 of 2010) and clearing house rules (2013 edition).

programs.title: Qatar | Payment Fraud Prevention for Electronic Transfers and Payment Services
programs.why: QCB requires banks to take care before executing transfer orders received from customers by electronic means, confirming them with the signatory or through secure e-banking with one-time passwords, and the Payment Services Regulation requires an effective fraud detection and resolution mechanism with cyber fraud controls for payment services. These are control duties that staff must understand; no training is prescribed.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (Arabic edition): Part One, Chapter Eleven: Miscellaneous Banking Matters
references.provision: Part One, Chapter Eleven, item 13 (transfer orders received electronically)
references.note: Banks must verify electronically received transfer orders by contacting the authorised signatory or through secure e-banking with one-time passwords (Circular 32/2015).

references.title: Payment Services Regulation (Licensing and Regulating Payment Service Providers)
references.note: Payment service providers, including banks for their payment services, need effective fraud detection and resolution covering digital transactions.

programs.title: Qatar | Occupational Health and Safety under the Labour Law
programs.why: The Labour Law requires employers to inform workers of work risks and protective measures when they start and to take safety precautions. The official texts could not be opened in this session (qcb.gov.qa sends an incomplete TLS certificate chain; qfiu.gov.qa, almeezan.qa and other .qa hosts refuse automated access), so the entry is not classified as mandatory.

references.title: Law No. 14 of 2004 on the promulgation of Labour Law
references.issuer: State of Qatar (Al Meezan legal portal)
references.provision: Chapter Ten (Safety, Occupational Health and Social Care)
references.note: Labour Law chapter on workplace safety; extracts say employers must tell workers about job risks and protective measures when they start work. Not opened: the Al Meezan portal now opens but serves its texts through a script-driven page that plain HTTP requests cannot read.

programs.title: Qatar | IFRS 9 Implementation under QCB Instructions
audience: Credit risk and ECL modelling staff
programs.why: QCB requires conventional banks to prepare financial statements under IFRS and to follow its implementing instructions for IFRS 9 on classification, measurement and expected credit loss, with periodic ECL reporting to QCB. Finance and credit risk staff must apply these instructions; no training duty is stated.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (Arabic edition): Part One, Chapter Seven, First: Monthly Statement and Final Accounts
references.provision: Part One, Chapter Seven, First, item 2/1 (International Accounting Standards)
references.note: Banks must follow QCB's instructions for applying IFRS 9 (Circular 9/2017) when preparing financial statements; the guidance itself is Annex 138 and ECL reporting forms Annex 139.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (Arabic edition): Annex 138, Guidance instructions for applying IFRS 9
references.note: QCB guidance on applying IFRS 9; the PDF opens but holds page images only, so its text could not be checked.

programs.title: Qatar | Accuracy of Prudential Reporting to QCB
programs.why: Under Circular 2/2024, board members and senior staff are responsible for the accuracy and timeliness of data sent to QCB. Banks need board-approved policies and three lines of defence over regulatory returns, must give the reporting functions qualified technical staff and systems, and face penalties for late or inaccurate data. This is a competence duty for reporting staff, without a set course.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (Arabic edition): Part Three: Periodic Data
references.provision: Part Three, Tenth (responsibility for accuracy of reports) and Eleventh (fines for late or inaccurate data)
references.note: Board and senior staff answer for accurate, timely returns; banks need policies, three lines of defence and qualified technical staff for reporting (Circular 2/2024), and fines apply for delays or errors (Circular 73/2010).

programs.title: Qatar | FATCA Compliance under the Qatar-US IGA
programs.why: Under the Qatar-US Model 1B IGA, brought into effect by QCB Circular 21/2015, QCB-regulated institutions must identify and document US accounts and report them to the QCB FATCA Unit. Operations and onboarding staff need this knowledge, but no training duty was found.

references.title: FATCA
references.note: QCB page on FATCA: Qatar and the US signed a Model 1B IGA on 7 January 2015, brought into effect by QCB Circular 21/2015; the Ministry of Finance is competent authority and QCB-regulated institutions report to the QCB FATCA Unit, which passes the data on for exchange with the IRS. Links guidance notes.

programs.title: Qatar | Common Reporting Standard Reporting to the General Tax Authority
programs.why: Reporting financial institutions must collect self-certifications and file CRS reports annually with the GTA, with penalties for failures. The official texts could not be opened in this session (qcb.gov.qa sends an incomplete TLS certificate chain; qfiu.gov.qa, almeezan.qa and other .qa hosts refuse automated access), so the entry stays at competence.

references.title: The Common Reporting Standard (CRS)
references.note: GTA page on CRS: the GTA is competent authority under Minister of Finance Decision No. 17 of 2019; reporting financial institutions file annually. Not opened: gta.gov.qa refuses automated access.

programs.title: Qatar | External Auditor Requirements and Audit Readiness
programs.why: QCB rules govern appointing and changing a bank's external auditor, the professional qualifications and experience the audit firm and its key staff must have, the auditor's duties and reports to QCB, and special assignments. Finance and audit committee members must manage the relationship and respond to findings; this is a competence duty.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (Arabic edition): Part One, Chapter Five: External (Statutory) Auditor
references.provision: Part One, Chapter Five, items 1 to 7
references.note: Appointment and change of auditor, conditions including professional qualifications and banking audit experience, duties, reports and special tasks.

references.title: Instructions to Banks (September 2013, fifteenth edition): Part VII, Chapter Six: External Auditor
references.note: Older English text of the external auditor chapter (2013 edition).

programs.title: Qatar | Investment Products and Services for Customers under QCB Instructions
programs.why: QCB rules cover banks' investment activity for customers: relationship with customers, internal controls, management and marketing of investment portfolios and funds (including third-party foreign funds), disclosure when promoting investment products, QCB no-objection before issue, and dealing for customers in foreign exchange, commodities and metals. Sales staff need to know these limits; no qualification is prescribed in the text checked.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (Arabic edition): Part One, Chapter Nine, First: Investments for Customers
references.provision: Part One, Chapter Nine, First, items 1 to 5
references.note: Investment business for customers, customer relationship and internal controls, portfolio and fund management and marketing, disclosure, QCB no-objection, foreign exchange and commodity dealing for customers.

programs.title: Qatar | Distributed Ledger Technology under the QCB DLT Guideline
programs.why: The QCB DLT Guideline (in force 22 July 2024) applies to any QCB-regulated entity using or proposing to use distributed ledger technology. It requires governance, risk assessment, outsourcing controls and a register, and says DLT adoption must be backed by staff with role-specific skills; staff running innovative technology are expected to have the expertise, supported by adequate training and educational material. The training element is worded as an expectation, so this stays at competence.

references.title: Distributed Ledger Technology Guideline (Regulating the use of Distributed Ledger Technology by QCB Licensed Entities)
references.note: Entities using DLT must have staff with the skills and knowledge their roles need, and should give adequate training and educational material on DLT risks.

programs.title: Qatar | Artificial Intelligence Governance under the QCB AI Guideline
programs.why: QCB issued Artificial Intelligence Guidelines (Circular 6/2024) that set conditions for banks using AI. The Instructions to Banks state that all banks must comply from the circular's date and bring their arrangements into line within one year, with penalties for breach. The guideline PDF itself is image-only and could not be read, so no specific staff training duty is confirmed.

references.title: Instructions to Banks 2024 (Arabic edition): Part One, Chapter Eleven: Miscellaneous Banking Matters
references.provision: Part One, Chapter Eleven, item 17 (Artificial Intelligence Guidelines)
references.note: Banks must comply with the AI Guidelines (Annex 160, Circular 6/2024 of 4 September 2024) and adjust within one year; breaches attract penalties under the QCB Law.

references.title: Artificial Intelligence Guideline
references.note: QCB guideline on AI use by financial institutions; search extracts mention training staff who work with AI systems on interpreting outputs, bias and limitations. The PDF opens but is image-only, so its text could not be checked.

notes: Law No. 20 of 2019 replaced Law No. 4 of 2010 as the AML/CFT law; Council of Ministers Decision No. 41 of 2019 issued its Implementing Regulations. The QFIU lists Decree-Law No. 19 of 2021 amending the law (Arabic text only), and its April 2024 STR instructions cite the law as amended in 2021.

Secondary sources report a Decree-Law No. 18 of 2025 amending Law 20 of 2019 to set up a national AML/CFT committee at the QCB and an independent FIU. The QFIU legislation page opened on 2026-11-08 does not list it, and it could not be confirmed against an official text.
The QCB AML/CFT Instructions for financial institutions (May 2020 edition) were opened on the QFIU site; no newer official edition was found.

The Instructions to Banks were reissued as a 2024 edition (Arabic only, chapters revised up to 2025) that replaces the September 2013 English edition still on the QCB site. It carries the governance instructions of Circular 25/2022 as amended by Circular 2/2023, which replaced the 2015 principles (Circular 68/2015), and Circular 2/2024 on board and senior staff responsibility for accurate reporting to QCB.

The QCB Cloud Computing Regulation entered into force on 15 April 2024. Later circulars added AI Guidelines (Circular 6/2024, binding with a one-year adjustment period), a digital banks framework (Circular 7/2024, December 2024), ESG supervisory principles (Circular 5/2024, reporting under Circular 6/2025) and a DLT Guideline (July 2024). The AI Guideline, eKYC Regulation (2023) and BNPL Regulation (2023) PDFs are image-only and could not be read.
The QFIU lists the targeted financial sanctions implementing decision as Decision No. 1 of 2020 (Arabic scan only); a Decision No. 59 of 2020 reported in search results could not be confirmed.

Access on 2026-11-08: qcb.gov.qa opened once its missing DigiCert intermediate certificate was supplied from DigiCert's official AIA host (full TLS verification kept), except the legislation index (401 Unauthorized) and the old AML page (redirects to an error page). qfiu.gov.qa opened. almeezan.qa and ncsa.gov.qa answer with script-driven pages whose texts could not be read; moci.gov.qa, gta.gov.qa and nctc hosts refused connections.
